question: According to the manual, studies show most crash-involved riders make which braking error?
choice_a: They never use the front brake at all
choice_b: They overbrake the front tire and underbrake the rear
choice_c: They underbrake the front tire and overbrake the rear
choice_d: They apply both brakes with exactly equal, moderate pressure
explanation: Studies show that most crash-involved riders underbrake the front tire and overbrake the rear, and often did not separate braking from swerving or did not choose swerving when it was appropriate.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.24, 'Crash Avoidance'

question: To make a quick stop, how should a rider apply the brakes?
choice_a: Pump both brakes rapidly on and off
choice_b: Use only the rear brake to avoid locking the front wheel
choice_c: Use only the front brake and ignore the rear entirely
choice_d: Apply both brakes at the same time, squeezing the front brake lever firmly and progressively without grabbing it
explanation: To stop quickly, apply both brakes at the same time. Don't be shy about using the front brake, but don't grab it -- squeeze the brake lever firmly and progressively while pressing down on the rear brake.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.24, 'Quick Stops'

question: If the front wheel locks during a quick stop, what should the rider do?
choice_a: Release the front brake lever immediately, then reapply it firmly
choice_b: Keep the front brake locked until the motorcycle stops completely
choice_c: Immediately release the rear brake instead
explanation: If the front wheel locks, release the front brake lever immediately then reapply it firmly. At the same time, press down on the rear brake.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.24, 'Quick Stops'

question: If a rider accidentally locks the rear brake on a good traction surface while the motorcycle is upright and going straight, what can they do?
choice_a: Immediately let go of both brakes and coast
choice_b: Keep the rear wheel locked until completely stopped -- it can still be controlled
choice_c: Downshift repeatedly until the wheel unlocks
choice_d: Swerve sharply to break the lock
explanation: If you accidentally lock the rear brake on a good traction surface, you can keep it locked until you have completely stopped; even with a locked rear wheel, you can control the motorcycle if it is upright and going in a straight line.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.24, 'Quick Stops'

question: If a rider must stop quickly while leaned over in a curve, what should they do first (if the situation allows)?
choice_a: Immediately swerve to the opposite direction
choice_b: Apply maximum front brake pressure while still fully leaned
choice_c: Straighten and square the handlebars, then stop
choice_d: Accelerate through the curve before braking
explanation: If you must stop quickly while in a curve, first straighten and square the handlebars, then stop; using both brakes in a turn is possible but should be done very carefully since less traction is available for stopping while leaned.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.24-25, 'Stopping Quickly in a Curve'

question: A swerve is best described as:
choice_a: Coming to a complete stop before changing direction
choice_b: A gradual lane change over several seconds
choice_c: A full application of both brakes simultaneously
choice_d: A sudden change in direction, made by applying a small amount of hand pressure toward the intended escape path
explanation: A swerve is a sudden change in direction. Apply a small amount of hand pressure to the handgrip on the side of your intended direction of escape; this causes the motorcycle to lean quickly.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.25, 'Swerving or Turning Quickly'

question: When swerving to avoid an obstacle, when should braking be combined with the swerve?
choice_a: It shouldn't be combined -- brake before or after, never while making an aggressive swerve
choice_b: Always brake hard during the swerve for maximum control
choice_c: Braking and swerving should always be done at the exact same instant
choice_d: Braking is unnecessary once a swerve has begun
explanation: If the situation allows, separate braking from swerving. Brake before or after -- never while making an aggressive swerve.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.25, 'Swerving or Turning Quickly'

question: What is the immediate consequence of a front-wheel skid?
choice_b: Immediate loss of steering control and balance
choice_c: No noticeable effect if speed is under 20 mph
choice_d: An automatic activation of ABS on all motorcycles
explanation: Front-wheel skids result in immediate loss of steering control and balance. If the front wheel locks, release the front brake lever immediately and reapply with less pressure -- failure to release immediately will result in a crash.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.26, 'Front-Wheel Skids'

question: What causes a rear-wheel high-side crash after a rear-wheel skid?
choice_a: The rider used engine braking instead of the brakes
choice_b: The front brake was applied too gently
choice_c: The rear wheel is out of alignment with the front, and a locked rear wheel is suddenly released, snapping the motorcycle upright
choice_d: The headlight beam was too dim to see the hazard
explanation: If the rear wheel is out of alignment with the front and a locked rear wheel is released, the motorcycle can abruptly snap upright, throwing the rider into the air ahead of the motorcycle's path -- even slight misalignment can result in a high-side crash.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.26, 'Rear-Wheel Skids'

question: According to the manual, a primary cause of single-vehicle crashes is:
choice_d: Motorcyclists running wide in a curve or turn
explanation: A primary cause of single-vehicle crashes is motorcyclists running wide in a curve or turn. Every curve is different, so riders should ride within their skill level and posted speed limits.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.26, 'Curves'

question: Before entering a curve, what does the manual suggest as a good lane-position choice?
choice_a: Move to the center of the lane and stay there until you exit the curve
choice_b: Move as far right as possible for the entire curve
choice_c: Ride the extreme outside edge of the lane through the whole curve
choice_d: Lane position doesn't matter in curves as long as speed is controlled
explanation: A good choice is to move to the center of your lane before entering a curve and stay there until you exit -- this permits you to spot approaching traffic as soon as possible and adjust for debris or traffic crowding the center line.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.26, 'Curves'

question: Why does the manual caution against using the front brake incorrectly on a slippery surface while cornering?
choice_a: The front brake has no effect at all on a slippery surface
choice_b: It may be hazardous, so the rider should use caution and squeeze the brake lever, never grab it
choice_c: It is only a concern for the rear brake, never the front
choice_d: Grabbing the front brake is the recommended technique on slippery curves
explanation: When leaning the motorcycle, some traction is used for cornering, leaving less traction available for stopping; a skid can occur if too much brake is applied, and using the front brake incorrectly on a slippery surface may be hazardous. Use caution and squeeze the brake lever -- never grab it.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.24, 'Stopping Quickly in a Curve'

question: In the last few feet before coming to a stop from a curve, what should a rider do with the handlebars?
choice_b: Keep the handlebars turned into the curve until fully stopped
choice_c: Always straighten the handlebars to maintain balance and remain upright
choice_d: Handlebar position in the final feet of stopping makes no difference
explanation: As you slow in a curve, you can reduce lean angle and apply more brake pressure; always straighten the handlebars in the last few feet of stopping to maintain your balance and remain upright.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.24, 'Stopping Quickly in a Curve'
